title: How AI systems work
desc: Follow the input → model → output pipeline with hands-on examples
content_html:
What We're Doing

Every AI system — whether it's a chatbot, an image generator, or a voice assistant — follows the same basic pattern: Input → Model → Output. Something goes in (a question, a photo, a sound), a trained model processes it, and something comes out (an answer, a label, a new image). In this activity, students will explore this pipeline hands-on using three different kinds of AI tools, tracing exactly what information goes in, what happens "inside the box," and what comes out. By the end, students will be able to draw and explain the input-model-output pipeline for any AI system they encounter, and they will have built a simple "AI pipeline map" poster or worksheet documenting their experiments.

This lesson deliberately uses multiple tools (text, image recognition, and text-to-image) so students see that the same three-stage pattern applies across very different types of AI, which builds a transferable mental model rather than a tool-specific skill.

Tools & Resources

  • ChatGPT (free tier) — https://chat.openai.com — text input/output chatbot. Free tier may require an account; occasional usage limits or "at capacity" messages during peak times.
  • Google Teachable Machine — https://teachablemachine.withgoogle.com — free, no login required; uses webcam for image classification. Needs camera access permission on the device.
  • Craiyon — https://www.craiyon.com — free text-to-image generator; no login needed, but image generation can take 30–60 seconds and quality is lower than paid tools (useful for discussing limitations!).
  • Printed or digital "Pipeline Map" worksheet (teacher-prepared: three boxes labelled Input / Model / Output with arrows between them).
  • Projector or shared screen for demonstrating each tool before students try independently.

Step-by-Step Activity

  1. Introduce the pipeline concept on the board: draw three boxes labeled INPUT → MODEL → OUTPUT. Explain that "Model" is the trained AI system that has learned patterns from huge amounts of data, and it transforms input into output based on those patterns.
  2. Give a simple non-digital example first: a vending machine. Input = coin + button press, "Model" = the machine's internal mechanism, Output = snack. Ask students to identify input/model/output in 2–3 everyday examples (e.g., a thermostat, Google Search).
  3. Demonstrate Station 1 — Text AI: Open ChatGPT and type the prompt: "Write a two-sentence story about a matatu that can fly." Ask students to identify: What was the input? What do we think the model did? What was the output?
  4. Have students (in pairs or small groups) take turns typing their own short prompt into ChatGPT and recording the input and output on their worksheet.
  5. Move to Station 2 — Image AI: Open Google Teachable Machine's pre-built demo or quickly train a mini model live (e.g., classify "hand open" vs "hand closed" using the webcam). Show students how the input (webcam image) is processed by the model and produces an output (a label with a confidence percentage).
  6. Ask students to test the model with unusual inputs (e.g., a different hand position, an object instead of a hand) and observe how the output changes or becomes less confident. Record observations.
  7. Move to Station 3 — Text-to-Image AI: Open Craiyon and enter the prompt: "a lion wearing sunglasses riding a bicycle in Nairobi". While it generates, ask students to predict what the output might look like.
  8. When the images appear, discuss: Did the output match expectations? What might the model have "misunderstood"? Record input and output on the worksheet.
  9. Students complete their Pipeline Map worksheet for all three tools, writing one sentence per tool explaining what the "model" part might be doing (e.g., "matching patterns in text it has seen before").
  10. Regroup as a class. Each pair shares one surprising input-output pair and discusses what this reveals about how the model works.
  11. Close with a whole-class recap: list all three tools on the board and co-create one shared definition of "model" based on the day's observations.

Example Outputs

  • Text AI example: Input: "Write a two-sentence story about a matatu that can fly." Output: "Every Monday, the matatu named Simba sprouted wings and soared over Nairobi traffic. Passengers paid extra for the aerial view of Uhuru Park." Student notes: "The model used words it has seen in stories before and combined them with my topic."
  • Image classification example: Input: webcam photo of an open hand. Output: "Open Hand — 92% confidence." Student notes: "When I showed a closed fist halfway, the model got confused and gave both labels close to 50%, showing it compares to patterns it learned."
  • Text-to-image example: Input: "a lion wearing sunglasses riding a bicycle in Nairobi." Output: a slightly distorted image showing a lion-like shape, sunglasses, and a bicycle-ish object, but with an extra wheel and oddly shaped paws. Student notes: "The model understood 'lion,' 'sunglasses,' and 'bicycle' separately but struggled to combine them correctly — it doesn't really 'know' what a lion riding a bike looks like."

Facilitation Tips

  • Rotate groups through the three stations in timed blocks (roughly 12–15 minutes each) rather than letting everyone use one device at once — this keeps pacing tight for a 60-minute session.
  • Pre-test all three tools and your internet connection before class; Craiyon image generation can be slow on weak connections, so consider pre-generating 1–2 backup images in case of downtime.
  • Students often confuse "model" with "the whole computer" or "the whole app" — reinforce that the model is specifically the trained pattern-matching part, while buttons, screens, and internet connections are just the delivery mechanism.
  • When outputs are strange, funny, or wrong, resist the urge to immediately explain — ask the students "why do you think it did that?" first to build their own reasoning.
  • Keep an eye on students typing inappropriate prompts into open text/image tools; consider pre-approving a prompt list or supervising screens closely during free exploration.
  • For classes without reliable internet or devices for every student, this activity works well as a teacher-led demonstration with students recording predictions and observations on paper.

Discussion Questions

  • What are the three main stages every AI system follows, and can you name an example of each from today?
  • Why did the image classifier sometimes give a low-confidence or wrong answer? What does that tell us about how it "thinks"?
  • Is the "model" the same thing as the input or the output? How would you explain the difference to a friend who missed class?
  • Do you think AI models truly "understand" what they produce, or are they finding patterns? What's the difference?
  • If you wanted to make the lion-and-bicycle image come out better, what would you change — the input, the model, or something else? Why?

Extension Challenges

  • Easy: Create a Pipeline Map for a familiar app on your phone (e.g., a camera's face filter or a music recommendation app), identifying its input, model, and output without using any new tools.
  • Medium: Run the same prompt through two different tools (e.g., ChatGPT and another free chatbot) and compare the outputs. Write three sentences explaining why the outputs might differ even though the input was identical.
  • Hard: Design an experiment to "break" one of today's models — find an input so unusual or tricky that the model gives a clearly wrong or low-confidence output. Document the input, output, and your hypothesis for why the model failed.
